title: In essentials, unity
hook: an old motto: in essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity

segments.voice: Yesterday, he will come again, and a prayer near the Bible's end. Your line was come, Lord Jesus.

In essentials, unity. In non-essentials, liberty. In all things, charity. Three short lines, sometimes lettered on a church wall or printed in a bulletin. People like to hang the motto on famous names; who first wrote it is less certain than the motto itself. What's clear is who it was written for: Christians who disagreed, sometimes bitterly, and still had to share a city, a table, a faith. After a block of honest disagreements, it's a good place to stand.

The idea is older than the motto. Paul faced it in his letter to Rome. Some believers ate meat; others ate only herbs. Some kept certain days as holy; others treated every day alike. They were starting to look down on each other. Paul's answer opens like this: "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations." Welcome each other, and don't turn the welcome into a debate. And then: "Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind." Food and days, for Paul, were not things to split over. Now the hard part. Who decides what counts as essential? Churches don't share one list. Some point to the creeds. Some to the plain teaching of scripture about Christ. Catholics and Orthodox to the teaching the church has received and handed on. Even the list of essentials is something Christians disagree about. Which is why the last line carries so much weight. In Paul's chapter on love, charity is the King James word for love, and the chapter is blunt: "though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing." All faith. Even right faith, on every essential. Without love, nothing. So the letter to the Ephesians asks for effort: "Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace." Unity there isn't a feeling that happens on its own. It's something kept, on purpose.

Choose one real disagreement, with a relative, a friend, a church, a stranger online, and ask: is this essential, or not? Whatever you decide, find one good thing the other person is trying to protect, and hold it a while without giving up your own view. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just wish them well.
In essentials. The first line of an old motto: unity on what matters most, liberty on the rest, and charity, which is love, over everything.
Your line: in all things, charity. The motto's last line, and its heaviest. Day one thousand one hundred ten.

howItsDone: Christians from different churches can be found working and praying together on what they hold in common, such as the creeds, the Lord's Prayer and service to neighbors, while keeping their own teaching on matters where they differ.

chat.says: My friend's church and mine disagree on lots. Can we still be Christians together?
options: An old motto says: unity on essentials, liberty on the rest, and charity, love, over everything.
Only if one of you gives up; Paul says believers must agree on every detail to share a table.
Yes, but only if you never talk about faith, since disagreeing is itself a sin for Paul.
chat.meaning: The motto asks for unity on what matters most, liberty on the rest, and charity in all. Paul says without love, even all faith is nothing.

notes: The motto is often attributed to Augustine; it is usually traced to a 17th-century Lutheran writer (Rupertus Meldenius). Per the claims rule the script names neither, saying only that its authorship is less certain than the motto. Confirm.

'Paul faced it in his letter to Rome': Romans 14 is addressed to Rome; whether the meat question there concerns idol meat or kosher scruples is debated, so the script says only 'uneasy about where it came from'. Confirm.
